etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English breken, from Old English brecan (“to break”), from Proto-West Germanic *brekan, from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”). The word is a doublet of bray.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To crack or fracture (bone) under a physical strain.
(transitive, intransitive) To separate into two or more pieces, to fracture or crack, by a process that cannot easily be reversed for reassembly.

quote.citation: 2012 May 8, Yotam Ottolenghi, Sami Tamimi, Ottolenghi: The Cookbook‎[3], Random House, →ISBN, page 79:
quote.text: First, marinate the tofu. In a bowl, whisk the kecap manis, chilli sauce, and sesame oil together. Cut the tofu into strips about 1cm thick, mix gently (so it doesn't break) with the marinade and leave in the fridge for half an hour.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To divide (something, often money) into smaller units.
To turn an animal into a beast of burden.

quote.citation: 2002, John Fusco, Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron:
quote.text: Colonel: See, gentlemen? Any horse could be broken.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause (a person or animal) to lose spirit or will; to crush the spirits of.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Job 9:16–17:
quote.text: If I had called, and had answered me, yet would I not beleeue that he had hearkened vnto my voice: For he breaketh me with a tempest, and multiplieth my wounds without cause.

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: An old man, broken with the storms of state,Is come to lay his weary bones among ye;Give him a little earth for charity

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be crushed, or overwhelmed with sorrow or grief.

quote.citation: 1986 February 1, Kathy Jo Elliott, “Solid As A Rock”, in Gay Community News, volume 13, number 28, page 5:
quote.text: Two days later they transferred her to another prison to separate us. I broke. My life was gone, so I thought.

definitions.definition: (transitive, theater) To end the run of (a play).

quote.citation: 1958, Walter Macqueen-Pope, St. James's: Theatre of Distinction, page 134:
quote.text: In July Alexander broke the run and went on tour, as was his custom. He believed in keeping in touch with provincial audiences and how wise he was!

quote.citation: 1986, Kurt Gänzl, The British Musical Theatre: 1865-1914, page 610:
quote.text: After Camberwell he broke the play's season and brought it back in the autumn with a few revisions and a noticeably strengthened cast but without any special success.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To interrupt; to destroy the continuity of; to dissolve or terminate.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: Go, release them, Ariel; / My charms I'll break, their senses I'll restore.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To ruin financially.

quote.citation: 1693, Decimus Junius Juvenalis, John Dryden, transl., “[The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis.] The Seventh Satyr”, in The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis. Translated into English Verse.  […]  Together with the Satires of Aulus Persius Flaccus. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: With arts like these rich Matho, when he speaks, / Attracts all fees, and little lawyers breaks.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, obsolete) To fail in business; to go broke, to become bankrupt.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Riches”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: He that puts all upon adventures doth oftentimes break, and come to poverty.

quote.citation: 1791-92, Jane Austen, ‘A Collection of Letters’, Juvenilia:
quote.text: ‘I knew he was in some such low way—He broke did not he?’

definitions.definition: (finance, intransitive) Of prices on the stock exchange: to fall suddenly.

quote.citation: 2008, George Angell, Small Stocks for Big Profits:
quote.text: With a few exceptions, stock prices tend to follow the overall market averages. When you have a market decline, therefore, many stocks share the same overall chart pattern. Prices break and go sideways for a period of time.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To violate; to fail to adhere to.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 48, lines 749–751:
quote.text: Out, out Hyæna; theſe are thy wonted arts, [...] To break all faith, all vows, deceive, betray,

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of a fever) To go down, in terms of temperature, indicating that the most dangerous part of the illness has passed.
(intransitive, of a spell of settled weather) To end.
(intransitive, of a storm) To begin or end.
(intransitive, of morning, dawn, day etc.) To arrive.

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Sixt”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: The day begins to break, and night is fled.

definitions.definition: (transitive, gaming slang) To render (a game) unchallenging by altering its rules or exploiting loopholes or weaknesses in them in a way that gives a player an unfair advantage.
(specifically, in programming) To cause (some feature of a program or piece of software) to stop functioning properly; to cause a regression.
(transitive, intransitive) To stop, or to cause to stop, functioning properly or altogether.
(specifically) To cause the shell of (an egg) to crack, so that the inside (yolk) is accessible.
(specifically) To open (a safe) without using the correct key, combination, or the like.
(transitive) To cause (a barrier) to no longer bar.

quote.citation: 1992, “Rain When I Die”, performed by Alice in Chains:
quote.text: I'm a riddle so strong, you can't break me

definitions.definition: (transitive) To destroy the arrangement of; to throw into disorder; to pierce.
(intransitive, of a wave of water) To collapse into surf, after arriving in shallow water.  A wave breaking.
(intransitive) To burst forth; to make its way; to come into view.

quote.citation: 1717, John Dryden, “Book I. [The Gyants War.]”, in Ovid’s Metamorphoses in Fifteen Books. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 16:
quote.text: The Clouds are ſtill above; and, while I ſpeak, / A ſecond deluge o'er our head may break.

quote.citation: 1800, William Wordsworth, The Fountain:
quote.text: And from the turf a fountain broke, / And gurgled at our feet.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To interrupt or cease one's work or occupation temporarily; to go on break.
(transitive) To interrupt (a fall) by inserting something so that the falling object does not (immediately) hit something else beneath.
(transitive, ergative) To disclose or make known an item of news, a band, etc.

quote.citation: 2010, Jon Kutner, Spencer Leigh, 1,000 UK Number One Hits:
quote.text: Herman's Hermits version of 'I'm Into Something Good' topped the UK charts and also broke the band in the States.

quote.citation: 2023 March 8, Jonathan Tannenwald, “CBS is launching a 24/7 soccer channel online”, in The Philadelphia Inquirer‎[4]:
quote.text: “If something breaks during the day, work hours up until the evening, we’ll cut in — if we’re in the middle of, let’s say, a magazine program or a podcast on tape or a re-air of the game,” Radovich said.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of a sound) To become audible suddenly.

quote.citation: c. 1843, George Lippard, The Battle-Day of Germantown, reprinted in Washington and His Generals "1776", page 45 [5]:
quote.text: Like the crash of thunderbolts[...], the sound of musquetry broke over the lawn, [...].

definitions.definition: (transitive) To change a steady state abruptly.
(transitive, with for) To (attempt to) disengage and flee to; to make a run for.

quote.citation: 2018 October 17, Drachinifel, 26:02 from the start, in Last Ride of the High Seas Fleet - Battle of Texel 1918‎[6], archived from the original on 4 August 2022:
quote.text: As the last firing of the big guns begins to die down, the German light forces still fighting to the west begin to make their choices.  Some break for the open sea; others run for the German-occupied coast; still others stand and die.  A small group decide to strike their colors, in imitation of three of the larger German ships.

definitions.definition: (copulative, informal) To suddenly become.
(intransitive, of a male voice) To become deeper at puberty.
(intransitive, of a voice) To alter in type due to emotion or strain: in men, generally to go up, in women, sometimes to go down; to crack.
(intransitive, of a sauce or emulsion) To de-emulsify.

quote.citation: 2004, J. L. Atwood, Jonathan W. Steed, Encyclopedia of supramolecular chemistry‎[7], volume 2, page 1466:
quote.text: Conversely, as the emulsion breaks and the system returns to the original state, energy is released.

quote.citation: 2006, Johan Sjöblom, Emulsions and emulsion stability‎[8], volume 22, page 400:
quote.text: When the droplets hit a solid wall the emulsion breaks instantly forming a bitumen on the wall and thus a layer up to 1 cm thick can be sprayed in one operation without requiring drying in between.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To surpass or do better than (a specific number); to do better than (a record), setting a new record.
(transitive, tennis) To win a game (against one's opponent) as receiver.

quote.citation: 2012 June 28, Jamie Jackson, “Wimbledon 2012: Lukas Rosol shocked by miracle win over Rafael Nadal”, in the Guardian‎[9]:
quote.text: Yet when play restarted the Czech was a train that kept on running over Nadal. After breaking Nadal in the opening game of the final set, he went 2-0 up and later took the count to 4-2 with yet another emphatic ace – one of his 22 throughout.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, billiards, snooker, pool) To make the first shot; to scatter the balls from the initial neat arrangement.
(transitive, backgammon) To remove one of the two men on (a point).
(sports and games):
(transitive, military, most often in the passive tense) To demote; to reduce the military rank of.

quote.citation: 1926, T.E. Lawrence, Seven Pillars of Wisdom, New York: Anchor, published 1991, page 167:
quote.text: Sir Reginald Wingate, High Commissioner in Egypt, was happy for the success of the work he had advocated for years. I grudged him this happiness; for McMahon, who took the actual risk of starting it, had been broken just before prosperity began.

quote.citation: 1953 February 9, “Books: First Rulers of Asia”, in Time:
quote.text: And he played no favorites: when his son-in-law sacked a city he had been told to spare, Genghis broke him to private.

quote.citation: 1968, William Manchester, The Arms of Krupp, Back Bay, published 2003, →ISBN, page 215:
quote.text: One morning after the budget had failed to balance Finanzminister von Scholz picked up Der Reichsanzeiger and found he had been broken to sergeant.

quote.citation: 2006, Peter Collier, Medal of Honor: Portraits of Valor Beyond the Call of Duty, Second Edition, Artisan Books, →ISBN, page 42:
quote.text: Not long after this event, Clausen became involved in another disciplinary situation and was broken to private—the only one to win the Medal of Honor in Vietnam.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To end (a connection); to disconnect.
(intransitive, sports) To counter-attack.

quote.citation: 2010 December 28, Kevin Darlin, “West Brom 1 - 3 Blackburn”, in BBC‎[10]:
quote.text: The Baggies almost hit back instantly when Graham Dorrans broke from midfield and pulled the trigger from 15 yards but Paul Robinson did superbly to tip the Scot's drive around the post.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To lay open, as a purpose; to disclose, divulge, or communicate.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: Katharine, break thy mind to me.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become weakened in constitution or faculties; to lose health or strength.

quote.citation: 1731, Verses on His Own Death, Jonathan Swift:
quote.text: See how the dean begins to break; / Poor gentleman he droops apace.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To destroy the strength, firmness, or consistency of.
(transitive) To destroy the official character and standing of; to cashier; to dismiss.

quote.citation: January 11, 1711, Jonathan Swift, The Examiner No. 24
quote.text: when I see a great officer broke.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To make an abrupt or sudden change; to change gait.
(intransitive, archaic) To fall out; to terminate friendship.

quote.citation: c. 1700 Jeremy Collier, On Friendship
quote.text: To break upon the score of danger or expense is to be mean and narrow-spirited.

definitions.definition: (computing) To terminate the execution of a program before normal completion.
(programming) To suspend the execution of a program during debugging so that the state of the program can be investigated.
(computing) To cause, or allow the occurrence of, a line break.
An instance of breaking something into two or more pieces.
A physical space that opens up in something or between two things.
An interruption of continuity; departure from or rupture with.

quote.citation: 2023 May 29, Jonathan Head, “Pita Limjaroenrat: Thai election upstart who vows to be different”, in BBC‎[11]:
quote.text: But the young activists of Move Forward outmanoeuvred the older party, and beat many of its candidates, with an imaginative, social media-based campaign offering voters a complete break with the past, and a different kind of political leadership.

definitions.definition: (UK, education) A time for students to talk or play between lessons.
A scheduled interval of days or weeks between periods of school instruction; a holiday.
A rest or pause, usually from work.
A short holiday.
A temporary split with a romantic partner.
An interval or intermission between two parts of a performance, for example a theatre show, broadcast, or sports game.

quote.citation: 2010 December 29, Chris Whyatt, “Chelsea 1 - 0 Bolton”, in BBC‎[12]:
quote.text: But they marginally improved after the break as Didier Drogba hit the post.

definitions.definition: A significant change in circumstance, attitude, perception, or focus of attention.
(finance) A sudden fall in prices on the stock exchange.

quote.citation: 1947, Reports of the Tax Court of the United States, volume 8, page 459:
quote.text: Following the invasion of France by the Germans in May of 1940, the securities markets experienced a break in prices.

definitions.definition: The beginning (of the morning).
An act of escaping.
(computing) The separation between lines, paragraphs or pages of a written text.

quote.citation: 2001, Nan Barber, David Reynolds, Office 2001 for Macintosh: The Missing Manual, page 138:
quote.text: No matter how much text you add above the break, the text after the break will always appear at the top of a new page.

definitions.definition: (computing) A keystroke or other signal that causes a program to terminate or suspend execution.
(programming) Short for breakpoint.
(British, weather) A change, particularly the end of a spell of persistent good or bad weather.
(tennis) A game won by the receiving player(s).
(billiards, snooker, pool) The first shot in a game of billiards.
(snooker) The number of points scored by one player in one visit to the table.
(soccer) The counter-attack.

quote.citation: 2010 December 28, Owen Phillips, “Sunderland 0 - 2 Blackpool”, in BBC‎[13]:
quote.text: Blackpool were not without their opportunities - thanks to their willingness to commit and leave men forward even when under severe pressure - and they looked very capable of scoring on the break.

definitions.definition: (golf) The curve imparted to the ball's motion on the green due to slope or grass texture.
(surfing) A place where waves break (that is, where waves pitch or spill forward creating white water).
(horse racing) The start of a horse race.

quote.citation: 1999, Jay Hovdey, Cigar: America's Horse, page 63:
quote.text: Cigar was distracted at the break and let his five opponents get the jump.

quote.citation: 2010, John Alexander, Exotic Wagering the Winning Way, page 60:
quote.text: Perhaps it stumbles to its knees at the break, effectively losing the race at the outset.

definitions.definition: The opening of packages of cards for a collectible card game, often for further distribution to paying customers.
(sports and games):
(dated) A large four-wheeled carriage, having a straight body and calash top, with the driver's seat in front and the footman's behind.
Alternative form of brake (“cart or carriage without a body, for breaking in horses”)
(equitation) A sharp bit or snaffle.

quote.citation: 1576, George Gascoigne, The Steele Glas:
quote.text: Pampered jades  […]  which need nor break nor bit.

definitions.definition: (music) A short section of music, often between verses, in which some performers stop while others continue.

quote.citation: 1937, Ivan T. Sanderson, Animal Treasure, page 233:
quote.text: The effect was weird, because with that intuitive sense possessed by the African, every drummer knew exactly when the “breaks” were coming, and whole banks of bass drums would drop out precisely on the beat.

definitions.definition: (music) The point in the musical scale at which a woodwind instrument is designed to overblow, that is, to move from its lower to its upper register.
(music) The transition area between a singer's vocal registers; the passaggio.

quote.citation: 1862, John Winebrenner, The Serephina, Or, Christian Library of Church Music‎[14], page 13:
quote.text: 34. Of the Registers of the Voice - All singers have observed that there are certain parts of the Vocal Scale where a break, as it is called, seldom fails to occur.

quote.citation: 2007, S. Anthony Frisella, The Baritone Voice: A Personal Guide to Acquiring a Superior Singing Technique‎[15], page 14:
quote.text: The point of division between the two vocal registers is most frequently referred to as the register’s break.

quote.citation: 2018, Karen Brunssen, The Evolving Singing Voice: Changes Across the Lifespan‎[16], page 76:
quote.text: Boys should continue in their high voice, across the break to the lower range, and end up with a voice that doesn’t have a break (Leck, 2009).

definitions.definition: (geography, chiefly in the plural) An area along a river that features steep banks, bluffs, or gorges (e.g., Upper Missouri River Breaks National Monument, US).
(obsolete, slang) An error. [late 19th–early 20th c.]

quote.citation: 1916, Ring W. Lardner, “Three Kings and a Pair”, in The Saturday Evening Post‎[17]:
quote.text: "Maybe he will some day," says the Missus, and then her and Bessie pretended like they'd made a break and was embarrassed.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Clipping of breakdown (the percussion break of songs chosen by a DJ for use in hip-hop music) and see also breakdancing.

definitions.definition: (music) A section of extended repetition of the percussion break to a song, created by a hip-hop DJ as rhythmic dance music.

quote.citation: 1994, “N.Y. State of Mind”, in Illmatic, performed by Nas:
quote.text: The smooth criminal on beat breaks / Never put me in your box if your shit eats tapes

definitions.definition: (music, slang) To B-boy; to breakdance.

quote.citation: 1985, “King of Rock”, performed by Run-DMC:
quote.text: Let the poppers pop and the breakers break / We're cool, cool cats, it's like that

definitions.definition: (rare, mainly historical or a misspelling) To brake.

quote.citation: 1951 July, R. E. G. Read, “From Bere Alston to Callington”, in Railway Magazine, page 482:
quote.text: Breaking heavily, now on a 1 in 39 gradient, the train makes as if to cross the Tamar at once, only to swing sharply to the right,  […] .
